title: The ENTIRE History of Rome in 15 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of Rome in 15 Minutes
description:
From a legend about twins and a wolf in 753 BC to a boy emperor quietly retired in 476 AD, this is the whole story of Rome: kings, a republic, Hannibal's elephants, Caesar's pirates, an emperor who taxed pee, and the day the Praetorian Guard sold the empire at auction. Every fact is checked against the ancient writers and modern historians, and legends are labelled as legends.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #rome #romanempire #juliuscaesar #animatedhistory

beats.say: March, 193 AD. The Roman Empire, the most powerful state on Earth, is about to be sold. At an auction.
The Praetorian Guard, the emperor's own bodyguards, have just killed the emperor Pertinax, and now they're taking bids.
Who wants to be emperor? Bids per soldier, please!
Twenty thousand sesterces each!
Twenty-five thousand! Right now!
According to Cassius Dio, Julianus didn't just nudge the price up. He jumped by five thousand in one go, shouting it and holding up the number on his fingers.
Sold, to the guy shouting from outside the wall!
Spoiler: this did not go well for him.
So how did the greatest empire in the world end up on the auction block? To answer that, we have to go back. Way back. Wolves-and-twins back.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of Rome in 15 Minutes

beats.say: So. Italy. More specifically, a few hills next to a river called the Tiber.
Roman legend says twin brothers, Romulus and Remus, were sons of the war god Mars, got abandoned as babies, and were nursed by a she-wolf.
Which, sure. Totally normal childhood.
When the twins grew up, they decided to build a city, but they could not agree on which hill.
The Aventine hill. Obviously.
The Palatine hill. Obviously!
They tried to settle it by watching the birds for a sign from the gods, and naturally both of them claimed they'd won.
In the most famous version, it ends with Romulus killing his own brother and naming the city after himself. Rome.
The traditional birthday is April twenty-first, 753 BC, with the year worked out by a Roman scholar named Varro about seven hundred years later.

show.label: Rome's traditional birthday
show.sub: worked out by Varro, centuries after the fact

beats.say: Archaeologists say people were living on those hills long before that, but hey, a wolf is a better story.
According to tradition, Rome was then ruled by seven kings, and the last one was called Tarquin the Proud. The nickname tells you how that went.
Around 509 BC, the Romans threw Tarquin out and swore they'd never have a king again.
Instead, they elected two consuls, who each served for just one year. Two bosses, so neither one could get too powerful. Genius. Mostly.
Rome was now a republic, steered by a senate full of rich men in togas who loved a long speech.
Then, around 387 BC, an army of Gauls from the north smashed a Roman army and sacked the city.
The Romans agreed to pay a thousand pounds of gold to make them leave, and when they complained that the Gauls' weights were rigged, the chief, Brennus, threw his sword onto the scales too.
And, according to Livy, he added two very rude words in Latin.

show.who: Brennus, as told by Livy, History of Rome 5.48

beats.say: Rome never forgot that. Over the next century or so, it fought and conquered its way across most of Italy.
Next, Rome bumped into Carthage, a rich trading city in North Africa, and the two of them fought three wars, called the Punic Wars.
In the second war, a Carthaginian general named Hannibal had a truly unhinged idea.
What if we attack Italy... from the top?
Over the Alps? With elephants?
Especially with elephants.
In 218 BC, he marched out of Spain, over the Pyrenees, across the Rhone river, and straight over the Alps, with thousands of soldiers and thirty-seven war elephants.
Snow, cliffs, landslides, angry mountain tribes. Britannica says that on the fifteenth day he came down into Italy with most of those elephants still with him.
Fun fact: historians still argue about which pass he actually used. Nobody has found the elephant footprints.
Then, in 216 BC at Cannae, he crushed an enormous Roman army. Ancient writers put the Roman losses at somewhere between about fifty and seventy thousand men.
But Rome just refused to quit. It kept raising new armies, and Hannibal spent about fifteen years in Italy without ever taking the city.
In 202 BC, the Roman general Scipio finally beat him at Zama in Africa, and in 146 BC Rome destroyed Carthage completely.
Rome was now the boss of the Mediterranean. And with nobody left to fight, the Romans started fighting each other.
Enter the most famous Roman of them all: Gaius Julius Caesar.
But first, a quick flashback to around 75 BC, because young Caesar has the best pirate story in all of history.
Sailing to the island of Rhodes to study public speaking, he was captured by pirates in the Aegean Sea.
He sent his companions off to raise the ransom money, so for weeks it was just Caesar, a doctor, two servants, and a boat full of pirates.
We're holding you for twenty talents of silver!
Twenty? Do you know who I am? Ask for fifty.
According to Plutarch, he was held for thirty-eight days, bossed the pirates around, told them to keep quiet while he napped, and made them listen to his poems.
You don't like my poems? Illiterate barbarians. I'm going to have you all executed, you know.
Ha! This guy is hilarious.
He was not joking. Once the ransom was paid, he raised a fleet, caught them, and had every one of them executed.
Anyway. Grown-up Caesar conquered Gaul, which is basically modern France, then in 49 BC led his army into Italy and won a civil war against his rival Pompey.
After one very quick war in the east, he summed it up in his victory parade with a sign that had just three words on it: I came, I saw, I conquered.
Eventually the senate named him dictator for life. And a lot of senators did not love the 'for life' part.
On the Ides of March, 44 BC, a group of senators, including his friend Brutus, surrounded him at a senate meeting and stabbed him to death.
And no, he probably never said 'Et tu, Brute?' That line comes from Shakespeare, sixteen hundred years later.
Suetonius says Caesar mostly said nothing at all, though some writers claimed he told Brutus, in Greek, 'You too, my child?'
The senators thought killing Caesar would save the republic. Instead, it caused even more civil wars.
The winner was Caesar's adopted son, Octavian, who was only eighteen when Caesar died, and who later beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC.
In 27 BC, the senate gave him a shiny new name, Augustus. He said he had restored the republic. He had actually just become the first emperor.
Emperor? Me? No, no. I'm just the first citizen.
He ruled for about forty years, and in 8 BC the month called Sextilis was renamed August in his honour.
He also rebuilt the city so thoroughly that his biographer made this famous claim.

show.text: He could justly boast that he had found it built of brick and left it in marble.

beats.say: His reign kicked off about two hundred years of relative calm, the Pax Romana. Which does not mean every emperor was a winner.
Take Caligula. Suetonius says he gave his favourite racehorse, Incitatus, a marble stall, an ivory manger and a jewelled collar, and that he supposedly planned to make the horse a consul.
Many historians think those stories were exaggerated by writers who hated him. Still, great horse.
Then there's Vespasian, who came out on top after a chaotic civil war in 69 AD, the Year of the Four Emperors, and who started building the Colosseum.
He needed money, so he got creative, and taxed the urine collected from Rome's public toilets, which people used for laundry and tanning leather.
Dad. A tax on pee? That's disgusting.
Smell this coin. Does it stink?
No?
And yet it comes from urine.
That exchange is in Suetonius, and it's where the saying 'money doesn't stink' comes from.
By 117 AD, under the soldier emperor Trajan, who was born in Roman Spain, the empire hit its biggest size ever.
It stretched from northern Britain to Egypt, and from Portugal all the way to Mesopotamia.
That's roughly five million square kilometres, ruled from one city.
And that city was huge. Rome itself may have had around a million people, the largest city of pre-industrial Europe. London only matched it around 1800.

show.label: People living in Rome (estimate)
show.sub: no European city matched it until London, about 1800

beats.say: The Romans built roads, aqueducts, and concrete so good that the Pantheon, rebuilt by the next emperor, Hadrian, still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome on the planet.
It has been a church since 609, and it's still in use. And in 2023, MIT researchers found one of the secrets: little lumps of lime in the mix that help seal up cracks when water seeps in.
Hadrian also decided the empire was big enough, gave up Trajan's newest conquests in the east, and in 122 AD started building a wall right across northern Britain.
Now, remember our auction? Let's see how Rome got there. It starts with Commodus, emperor until 192, who loved fighting as a gladiator in the arena.
The senator and historian Cassius Dio watched from the stands, and says Commodus paid himself a million sesterces from the gladiator fund for every day he fought.
Once, after killing an ostrich in the arena, he walked up to the senators and just grinned at them, as if to say: you're next.
Don't laugh. Whatever you do, do not laugh.
Dio says they were all trying so hard not to laugh that he chewed the laurel leaves from his own wreath, and told the senators around him to do the same.
Commodus was assassinated in 192. The next emperor, Pertinax, lasted just eighty-seven days before his own guards killed him.
And then came that auction. Here's how Dio, who was actually in Rome at the time, described it.

show.text: Just as if it had been in some market or auction-room, both the City and its entire empire were auctioned off.

beats.say: The winning bid was twenty-five thousand sesterces for every single guardsman.
But generals out in the provinces had armies too, and one of them, Septimius Severus, marched on Rome.
After just sixty-six days on the throne, Julianus was killed in the palace. Dio says his last words were: 'But what evil have I done?'
Buddy, you bought an empire at a yard sale.
And it got messier. Between 235 and 284, at least twenty-six men claimed to be emperor, one emperor, Valerian, was captured by the Persians, and for a while the empire split into three.
Then the fixers showed up. In 293, the emperor Diocletian split the job between four rulers, because one person clearly could not handle it.
Then came Constantine, who won the battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312, gave Christians freedom of worship the next year, and became the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity.
On May eleventh, 330 AD, he dedicated a brand-new capital on the site of the old Greek city of Byzantium, and named it after himself: Constantinople, today's Istanbul.
Naming the city after yourself? Romulus would be proud.
By 395, the empire was being run as two halves, east and west, each with its own emperor. And only one of those halves was in real trouble.
In 410, Alaric and the Visigoths sacked Rome for three days, the first time in almost eight hundred years the city had fallen to a foreign enemy.
The western emperor, Honorius, wasn't even there. His court was safe in Ravenna, far away in the north-east of Italy.
Emperor! Roma has perished!
What? But she was eating out of my hand just now!
Not your chicken, sir. The city.
Oh. Phew.
That story, about a pet chicken named Roma, comes from the historian Procopius, and it's almost certainly made up. But it tells you what people thought of Honorius.
Finally, in 476, a Germanic general named Odoacer marched into power in Italy and deposed the boy usually counted as the last emperor of the west, Romulus Augustus.
People called him Augustulus, 'little Augustus'. And yes, his name combined the founder of Rome and its first emperor. History has jokes.
Keep your pension, kid. I'll just be King of Italy.

Odoacer didn't even bother calling himself emperor. He sent the imperial regalia off to the emperor in Constantinople, and let the boy retire on a pension to a fortress near Naples, where he may have lived for decades.
So is that the end of Rome? Not exactly.
The eastern half, which still called itself the Roman Empire, kept going for nearly another thousand years, until Constantinople fell in 1453.
From a wolf legend to a boy emperor with a pension, that's more than twelve hundred years. Not bad for a village on a few hills.
If Rome's wars felt ridiculous, wait until you see our next video: the most ridiculous wars in history. See you there.
